Hopefully that is, we're still gathering the data, but I do think there's something to the work. You want to build up robust, resilient players.
clips.news_angle: Taylor Jenkins on managing player health and workload
clips.social_post: Taylor Jenkins explains the team's intentional approach to practice structure and workload management to build robust and resilient players.

clips.speaker: Chris Mannix
clips.text: The Celtics have fallen off a cliff during this four-game West Coast road trip. They are 0-4, with losses to Golden State without Steph Curry, and Sacramento, which is generally bad. The offense has completely cratered around Jason Tatum. Paul George's numbers have dipped, Payton Pritchard's numbers have fallen off, and Derrick White still cannot buy a bucket from beyond the three-point line.
clips.news_angle: Celtics' offensive struggles during their four-game West Coast road trip
clips.social_post: The Celtics are struggling on their West Coast road trip with an 0-4 record. Chris Mannix notes the offense has cratered around Jayson Tatum as secondary options like Paul George and Derrick White struggle to find their rhythm.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: The offense has completely cratered around Jason Tatum.

clips.speaker: Evan Turner
clips.text: They are aware, but I don't think they are really concerned because it goes back to that age-old adage of, you live by the three, you die by the three, and I think that's the philosophy for the Boston Celtics. You look at the past two games, they have only lost by a total of two points. Of course, you want to win in Denver, and Denver has been playing at a high level. And then you caught a hot Magic team. Franz Wagner is playing unbelievable. But I think one thing that occurs is you pay attention to their defensive rating, and they are still doing enough to stop guys. They are still doing enough to stop teams and doing enough to win, but it is all about, do you want to be more versatile offensively? It has always been a complaint of guys shooting too many threes. I think they are hoisting 51 threes per game during that four-game skid, and shooting probably around 28%. So, I think if you went into that locker room, you would bet on your guys stepping up and making shots as opposed to them not making shots. Payton Pritchard did not have a good few games. You mentioned Paul George kind of dipping, and they are relying so heavily on Jason Tatum to playmake. But at the same time, I believe those other two guys will show up, but definitely need to see something more than Derrick White. What do you think? Do you think it is the team's situation, or is it just, hey, live by the three, die by the three? And would you change it?
clips.news_angle: Celtics' reliance on three-point shooting despite recent poor performance
clips.social_post: Evan Turner on the Celtics offensive philosophy: They are hoisting 51 threes per game during their skid while shooting around 28 percent. He believes the team is not overly concerned despite the recent losses.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: You live by the three, you die by the three, and I think that's the philosophy.

clips.speaker: Chris Mannix
clips.text: I am concerned about Derrick White. Derrick White's shooting is not a short-term thing. He has been in steady decline over the last year and a half. That is concerning to me. I think Payton Pritchard will figure it out, and they need him to figure it out because he is a shot creator for that team. But Derrick White's shooting numbers, that is a real problem for this team because as good as he is defensively, and as solid as he is as a playmaker, he has to make open shots. If he is open beyond the three-point line and he cannot be shooting sub-30%, that to me is a real concern.
clips.news_angle: Concerns regarding Derrick White's shooting slump and its impact on the Celtics
clips.social_post: Chris Mannix is raising concerns about Derrick White, noting his shooting has been in a steady decline over the last year and a half. He emphasizes that White must make open shots to remain effective for the Celtics.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: Derrick White's shooting is not a short-term thing. He has been in steady decline over the last year.

clips.speaker: Evan Turner
clips.text: I think his confidence has been affected. You look at the Sacramento game, he had at least two or three seconds to drive that ball, attack, and try to make a play. I feel as though, ever since last season, he has been trying to find his shot and kind of been inside his head. But it is so necessary because, like we said prior, you cannot rely on a 36, 37-year-old Paul George to be shooting and playing out of his mind, averaging mid-20s. He has been a great 3-and-D guy. He will be a great third option, but I think Derrick White definitely has to step up in order for this team to be anything, space the floor, but at the same time, take pressure off Jason Tatum.
clips.news_angle: Impact of Paul George's shooting slump on the Celtics' offensive rhythm
clips.social_post: Evan Turner believes Paul George's confidence has been affected during his shooting slump. He notes that while George is a great 3-and-D option, the Celtics need him to step up to take pressure off Jayson Tatum.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: His confidence has been affected. He had at least two or three seconds to drive that ball.

clips.speaker: Chris Mannix
clips.text: Teams are going to continue to do this to Tatum. They are going to continue to pressure him, to blitz him, to send double teams at him. And if you look at some of the numbers, it is having an effect. In his first 12 games, Tatum averaged 7.3 assists per game, a very good number. In the last three, he is down to 4.3. Turnovers, first 12 games, 2.7. Last three, five. Assist-to-turnover ratio, obviously not as good. 2.7 the first 12 games, less than one, 0.86 over the last three. Teams are just going to try everything they can to take the ball out of Tatum's hands. And if Derrick White is not making shots, if Pritchard is not making shots, if Paul George is not making shots, if Sam Hauser is not making shots, they are going to keep doing it.
clips.news_angle: Opposing teams' defensive strategies to pressure Jayson Tatum
clips.social_post: Opposing teams are successfully pressuring Jayson Tatum, leading to a spike in turnovers and a dip in assists over the last three games. Chris Mannix notes that teams will keep blitzing him until other Celtics start hitting shots.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: Teams are going to continue to do this to Tatum. They are going to continue to pressure him.

clips.speaker: Chris Mannix
clips.text: Let's do a state of the 76ers check-in here. Right now, they are 14-4. If you asked anybody in the 76ers front office if they could be 14-4 around Thanksgiving, they would be pretty ecstatic. Joel Embiid, not the same guy overall in terms of offense, but defensively he is getting the job done. He has been a stopper for them. Their defensive rating with Embiid is around 98. With Embiid off the floor, it is about 112. So, he has been a difference-maker for that team.
clips.news_angle: State of the 76ers and Joel Embiid's defensive impact
clips.social_post: The Sixers are 14-4 and Joel Embiid is making a massive impact on the defensive end. Chris Mannix notes the team's defensive rating is significantly better when Embiid is on the floor.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: Joel Embiid, not the same guy overall in terms of offense, but defensively he's getting the job done.

clips.speaker: Chris Mannix
clips.text: For all the talk about who is going to take the last shot, would there be dysfunction there, they are 10-0 in clutch games this season. So, that's been good. The analytic numbers, the deeper dive into them, not necessarily good. They are 10th in the NBA in offensive rating, that's good but not great. They are 10th in the NBA in defensive rating, good but not great. 12th in the NBA in net rating, good but not great.
clips.news_angle: 76ers' success in clutch situations and their offensive/defensive ratings
clips.social_post: The Sixers are 10-0 in clutch games this season, but Chris Mannix points out that their deeper analytic numbers are just good, not great, across offensive and defensive ratings.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: They are 10-0 in clutch games this season. So, that's been good.

clips.speaker: Evan Turner
clips.text: I see glass half full. I actually like everything they're doing to be completely honest with you. I like how they're aware of each other. They're trying to make it work. There's been certain games where you'll sit there and it's not always beautiful, but you're like, bro, they're moving the ball around beautifully. They're making sure everybody's getting touches. I feel as though even how V.J. Edgecombe is playing. I feel like that that camaraderie is kind of moving towards togetherness. There was a moment where Joel Embiid was kind of like, I don't know what's going on here, there, but I think that kind of got cleaned up. And I like where they're at personally. I mentioned the decline of Derrick White to keep it focused on him for a second. 23-24, the year the Celtics won the championship, he shot 46% from the field, close to 40% from three. That was like a high-water mark for Derrick White. That's when it's like, all right, this guy is the best third or fourth option in the NBA. The following season, 44%, 38%. Still good. Still good numbers. Last season, 39.4 from the field, 32.7 from three. This year, so far, 41% from the field, 28.9% from three. So this has basically been a steady decline for four years now.
clips.news_angle: Evan Turner's positive assessment of the 76ers' team chemistry and play
clips.social_post: Evan Turner likes the current chemistry of the Sixers, noting that they are moving the ball well and making sure everyone gets touches. He feels the team has cleaned up early season confusion.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: I like everything they're doing to be completely honest with you. I like how they're aware of each other.

clips.speaker: Evan Turner
clips.text: No way did I think they were going to survive without Anthony Edwards in that lineup. Well, they have not only survived, they have thrived. And they have done it with one of the best defenses in the NBA. They are number one, number two, or number three in a lot of defensive categories. They have been that good across the board on that end of the floor.
clips.news_angle: Timberwolves' resilience and defensive performance despite Anthony Edwards' injury
clips.social_post: The Timberwolves have thrived without Anthony Edwards, relying on one of the best defenses in the NBA. Evan Turner says the team has been impressive across the board on that end of the floor.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: No way did I think they were going to survive without Anthony Edwards in that lineup.

clips.speaker: Evan Turner
clips.text: I think one thing I make of the Timberwolves is just energy. I think just toughness. Like they they lost their star player and I feel as though their camaraderie, they're all together like really, really believing in each other. You look at LaMelo Ball, you see them screaming out, like I've never seen them play this much defense. I've never seen how he's been able to change, but also play at an All-Star level all while the guys have been out. You look at Kyle Anderson, he's been balling. You look at Jonathan Kuminga, what they're able to do with him, they got him to buy in and then you have Rudy Gobert as a solid, solid foundation. And I think Jaden McDaniels has gone from the conversation like 3-and-D to elite now, you know, two-way scorer, two-way defender. I mentioned the decline of Derrick White to keep it focused on him for a second. 23-24, the year the Celtics won the championship, he shot 46% from the field, close to 40% from three. That was like a high-water mark for Derrick White. That's when it's like, all right, this guy is the best third or fourth option in the NBA. The following season, 44%, 38%. Still good. Still good numbers. Last season, 39.4 from the field, 32.7 from three. This year, so far, 41% from the field, 28.9% from three. So this has basically been a steady decline for four years now.
clips.news_angle: Timberwolves' team chemistry and defensive intensity as key factors for success
clips.social_post: Evan Turner praises the Timberwolves energy and camaraderie in the absence of their star. He highlights Jaden McDaniels' growth into an elite two-way player as a key factor in their success.
clips.video_title: Celtics BAD Road Trip // Sixers Check-In // Injured Wolves Keep Winning | Chris Mannix & Evan Turner
clips.pull_quote: I think one thing I make of the Timberwolves is just energy. I think just toughness.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: We were roommates and we were playing. It was very interesting because my first interaction with him was before school started. We went over to the court and there was a dude over there. He had on street shoes and he was dunking on people. That was my first introduction to him as Dr. J. I seen him play and learning how to play the game at a high level, seen his evolution. He was like Michael Jordan before Michael Jordan because he had such a presence that we could not go anywhere on campus without drawing a crowd.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on his first impression of Julius Erving at UMass
clips.social_post: George Mumford on his first impression of Dr. J: He was like Michael Jordan before Michael Jordan. We could not go anywhere on campus without drawing a crowd.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: I seen him play and learning how to play the game at a high level.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: He was playing in a system, nothing ran for him, but when he went hardship, that is when things changed. He played his first semi-pro game. He was like Michael Jordan before Michael Jordan because he had such a presence. He was playing, he was just like an artist. He was doing stuff and I am saying, man, he is making that stuff up in real time. But that is what happens when you are in the flow, when you are in the zone. You have your basic fundamentals, but I felt like he could really express himself.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on Julius Erving's development as a player
clips.social_post: George Mumford on watching Julius Erving play: He was just like an artist. He was making stuff up in real time. That is what happens when you are in the flow.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: He was like Michael Jordan before Michael Jordan because he had such a presence.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: Phil was talking to John and he said that he wanted somebody to come in and help the guys deal with the stress of success because they had just won two NBA championships in a row. This was exactly 33 years ago. They came across me and they realized I was a room with Dr. J, so I had been around the league. I grew up like most other guys in the city. So I was invited to come to training camp in 1993. That began our more than 30-year relationship.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on how he began working with Phil Jackson
clips.social_post: George Mumford on how he started with the Bulls: Phil Jackson wanted someone to help the guys deal with the stress of success after winning back to back championships. That began our 30 year relationship.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: Phil was talking to John and he said that he wanted somebody to come in.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: Phil wanted somebody else to come in that would not have the positional power like he had, but somebody to come in and teach the guys how to deal with the stress of success. So that was me. I came in and I started talking about being a spiritual warrior and being in the zone. People are all about the zone or being in flow, and so that is how I introduced it. You have to have a certain level of audacity to go and talk to a championship team that just won three in a row and think you can help them.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on his coaching philosophy with Phil Jackson's teams
clips.social_post: George Mumford on joining the Bulls: You have to have a certain level of audacity to go and talk to a championship team that just won three in a row and think you can help them.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: I came in and I started talking about being a spiritual warrior and being in the zone.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: It was pretty much immediate. Because I had a lot of street cred, you know, room with Dr. J, come on, man. Being around him, I had the street cred and then I was able to deliver the goods and help them be able to play because one of the things that happened when I first got there was a crisis. I talked to them and I said, okay, there is two meanings of a crisis. One is danger and the other one is opportunity. So I said, we can sit here and let us focus on the opportunity.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on his immediate impact with the Bulls
clips.social_post: George Mumford on his early days with the Bulls: I had a lot of street cred because I roomed with Dr. J. When a crisis hit, I told them there are two meanings of a crisis: danger and opportunity.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: I had a lot of street cred, you know, room with Dr. J, come on, man.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: He was all about what I was doing and if you were to ask him, he will say that I saved his life by changing his leadership style. Because I talked to him about meeting them where they were and what I was doing was I could help him explain why he was doing things so he could take his game to another level, but also how important it was to have everybody else raise their game to the awareness. Because in the triangle system, it is a read, man. You have to be able to see things and respond.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on his impact on Phil Jackson's leadership
clips.social_post: George Mumford on Phil Jackson: If you ask him, he will say I saved his life by changing his leadership style. I helped him explain why he was doing things so he could take his game to another level.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: I saved his life by changing his leadership style.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: He has got too much energy. He is vibrating at a high level, so he does not need that much sleep. That is what it is. When you are in the moment and when you are present and you are not wasting time on the negative thoughts and all of that energy, that you have access to a lot of energy and he had a lot of energy. That was just because he was vibrating at a different level.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on Michael Jordan's energy levels
clips.social_post: George Mumford on Michael Jordan: He has got too much energy. He is vibrating at a high level, so he does not need that much sleep. He was not wasting time on negative thoughts.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: He has got too much energy. He is vibrating at a high level.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: I met Kobe before I started working with the Lakers. My impression of Kobe was he is the closest thing to MJ in terms of his tenacity and his willingness to work and his desire to be the greatest.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on his first impression of Kobe Bryant
clips.social_post: George Mumford on his first impression of Kobe Bryant: He is the closest thing to MJ in terms of his tenacity and his willingness to work and his desire to be the greatest.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: He is the closest thing to MJ in terms of his tenacity and his willingness to work.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: In 2015, he invited me to hang out with him for a week and I came and I talked to him and I realized that he remembered everything I taught him. I do not know if you remember, but after the game you came into the locker room with your two kids. I was with him. I was hanging out with him when you came in. We just vibe. We were a lot closer than most people know because you know, I work on the down low, you know. People do not know. I was the secret weapon for years because people do not want to know, they do not want to give up that they are doing this.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on Kobe Bryant's memory and work ethic
clips.social_post: George Mumford on his relationship with Kobe: We were a lot closer than most people know. I was the secret weapon for years because people do not want to give up that they are doing this work.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: He invited me to hang out with him for a week and I realized that he remembered everything.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: It is what I would call my effort. It is this ability to generate enough energy to get beyond low energy. Enthusiasm is really important and persistence. This continuous application of energy. This balance, you know, not too high, too low, but it is just like slow is smooth and smooth is fast. Slow motion gets you there quicker. You never stop. You just keep going, keep going, keep going, keep going. You return, you begin again, begin again, begin again, begin again. And what happens is every creates energy. That is why MJ has so much because he pushes through. So we have this idea of a second wind, right? And people do not realize the second wind you push beyond that, you have another, but you can go as high as 13 second winds and you can keep moving. And this is not just me saying it. The psychologist William James said that years ago. He said that the energy is a man, he wrote a book about it, but you can keep moving. But the idea is you cannot entertain the negative energy zapping thoughts.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on the 'Mamba Mentality' and flow state
clips.social_post: George Mumford on the Mamba Mentality: It is this continuous application of energy. Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. You never stop. You just keep going.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: You can go as high as 13 second winds and you can keep moving.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: It was 2000 and this one I talk about all the time, but it is pre-game and I am watching them work out and whatnot. I have my session with the team before that. My thing is, you know how it is, everybody has their routine. I do not really like to mess with people when they are pre-gaming and whatnot, but I am observing Kobe doing warm-ups and dude is like, it is like two points is worth 35. He is just really trying hard. So I walked over to him and I said, hey Kobe, the best way to score is not to try to score. And he had 16 points in the first quarter.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on Kobe Bryant's pre-game warm-up
clips.social_post: George Mumford on Kobe: I saw him overworking in warmups, so I told him the best way to score is not to try to score. He went out and had 16 points in the first quarter.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: The best way to score is not to try to score.

clips.speaker: George Mumford
clips.text: If you do not have a goal and you just be open and let the game come to you, just be present and then in the presence and just being alert and relaxed, then you are going to see way more opportunities. Which he did, he had 16 points in the first quarter without trying.
clips.news_angle: George Mumford on the importance of being present and relaxed
clips.social_post: George Mumford on the flow state: If you do not have a goal and you just be open and let the game come to you, you are going to see way more opportunities.
clips.video_title: The Man Phil Jackson Trusted With Michael Jordan & Kobe
clips.pull_quote: If you do not have a goal and you just be open and let the game come.

clips.speaker: God Shammgod
clips.team: Cousins with Vince Carter & Tracy McGrady
clips.text: It is funny that we have this conversation because every time somebody does a variation of the move they call Shammgod, people act like I jumped on some podcast before the game and said, 'Yo, I am going to do the Shammgod, y'all going to love it.' It is funny when people come at me and say, 'Well, somebody did something like this.' I laugh because I have done every variation that ever been put on video. The difference is the kids now and us growing up, we knew how to dribble, we did not know how to do moves. Whatever the defense did, that is what you reacted to. The problem now is no matter if I back all the way in the paint, you are euro-stepping. That makes no sense. Just doing the move just to do it. If I am playing you to the left, you worked on left-to-right cross, so you are going to cross no matter what when you could just go left. When people do a move and say, 'Oh, he upgraded this, he upgraded that,' I am like, 'No, you know how many times I practiced those things with my friends before 97?' In that game, that was what was called for. I was actually trying to do something else and he reacted, so I reacted.
clips.news_angle: God Shammgod on the origin and evolution of his signature move

clips.channel_team: Cousins with Vince Carter & Tracy McGrady

clips.speaker: Paul Pierce
clips.text: I was born in Oakland, but my basketball journey started in Los Angeles. I moved to LA when I was around fifth grade. At the time, I was a football and baseball player. But the LA culture, all the little kids in the neighborhood played basketball. That's when my basketball journey began because the new friends I met, they played ball. The thing to do on the Saturday when you were outside was to go to the park and hoop. That's how I started getting more and more into basketball because none of my friends played baseball or football. I started at the Inglewood YMCA, and the rest is history.
clips.news_angle: Paul Pierce on his basketball journey starting in Los Angeles

clips.video_title: Paul Pierce on Doc Rivers’ Mind Games, Story Behind “The Truth” & Pressures of Early Success

clips.speaker: Paul Pierce
clips.text: The Inglewood YMCA is legendary. You got guys like Darren Davis, Andre Miller, Jason Hart, Milton Palacio. We got about four or five pros all running at the same time frame. We all played at the same time at the Y. That was early 90s, and that was my first organized basketball. I was in the sixth grade, and I played up. I was coming off the bench. That was the start of my basketball journey.

clips.speaker: Paul Pierce
clips.text: My biggest influence was my mom. She was like, you're not no follower. You got to do stuff that you want to do. Don't do stuff that everybody else is doing. Be your own man, make your own decisions. Don't make a decision based on what other people do or whatever people think. And that really stuck with me. Just because he was doing it, why I got to do that? Especially if it negatively impacted me. I did play basketball because of my friends, but that's something positive. That's sports. That's teaching you the game of life. That's what basketball was able to do, teach me the game of life. It taught me hard work, discipline, teamwork, everything I use in life today.
clips.news_angle: Paul Pierce's mother taught him to be a leader, not a follower
clips.social_post: Paul Pierce credits his mother for teaching him to be a leader rather than a follower, a mindset that helped him navigate the pressures of the NBA and stay true to himself throughout his career.

Now it's normal to play varsity as a freshman. But in my era, if you played junior varsity as a freshman, you were doing good. I made the team, but I didn't get no minutes at first. Just to be a freshman on junior varsity, that was a big deal. But then I wasn't even playing, so that was kind of discouraging because I was just like, I'm not even developing. I'm pretty much just watching the games, practicing, and it almost got to the point where my basketball career was going to be over.

clips.speaker: Jimmer Fredette
clips.text: I wouldn't necessarily say it was sharpening my game, but what it did do is make me mentally prepared for anything. My next-door neighbor, he used to run the rec portion of two different prisons in upstate New York. So he was like, for the inmates that are going to be on good behavior, he asked my dad and my brother, would you be interested in playing some ball and just bringing some guys up? And I was probably too young to be in there, so I had to have parental consent to actually go in. You'd walk straight through and then you'd get into the gym. There'd be no one there at first, but there'd be prison guards with their guns at each corner. And then all of a sudden they open the door and inmates would come in and they would watch on the bleachers. They'd start betting. At first, they were always betting against us, right? Because we don't look like we're great basketball players when we walk into the gym. And they start betting against us and they're cheering against us, cheering for their guys. And then all of a sudden we start playing and we start hitting some shots and all these different things and it completely changes. 180, they're betting for us now and they're cheering for us all the whole time.
clips.news_angle: Jimmer Fredette on playing against prisoners as a young player

It wasn't like I could watch Syracuse or North Carolina or UConn, right? You can see all of those games all the time. So I was like, all right, let's do it, let's go out. So I just went to a generic basketball camp. Most of the time, kids are going and being babysat, right? It's not an actual elite camp. clips.speaker: Jimmer Fredette
clips.text: Elder Ballard is the quorum of the 12 apostles for our church, so he's very, very high up in the church. He called me one day and was like, hey, Jimmer, just wanted to check in. And obviously that was my rookie season and things weren't going well, and I was down for sure, and it was a difficult situation. And he just kind of listened to me vent to him for 30 minutes, 40 minutes, whatever it was, telling him how the situation, I don't know what to do, things aren't going well, blah, blah, all these different things. And he just basically challenged me. He's like, hey, Jimmer, I have one question for you. He said, are you reading your scriptures daily? And at that point, I really wasn't, and I was focusing on just all basketball-related things. He's like, well, listen, you got to change your mindset, start reading your scriptures daily, and really, really diving into them, and focusing in on serving others and doing things, and I promise you if you do that, things will get better.
clips.news_angle: Jimmer Fredette on Elder Ballard's mentorship during his struggles
clips.social_post: Jimmer Fredette on his rookie struggles: Elder Ballard called me and told me to stop focusing only on basketball, change my mindset, and start reading my scriptures daily.

clips.pull_quote: He said, are you reading your scriptures daily? And at that point, I really wasn't.

clips.speaker: Jimmer Fredette
clips.text: Mike Conley Jr. When I first saw Mike, I didn't know much about Mike Conley. He went to Ohio State for like a year, maybe, and then he came out and he went to Memphis. And they had Z-Bo, Marc Gasol, Rudy Gay, Tony Allen. Like they had a really, really good team, obviously the grit and grind. Tony Allen used to love guarding me. Every single time I came into the game, Tony's like, I got him. Every single time. It was hilarious. But Mike, I didn't know much about him, and that he was a pest defensively. He was incredible in ball screens, but the thing about him that was hard was he was a left-hander, but he could shoot it better floaters with his right hand. So because of that, you're guarding him to go right because you want to force him to his left to his right hand because he's left-handed, but he was better going that direction. So you're like, wait, I got to switch my mindset, I got to try to make, but he was just an awesome player. He shot such a great percentage from the three, from the two, and he was a guy, and he was a great person.
clips.news_angle: Jimmer Fredette on Mike Conley Jr. as a tough opponent
clips.social_post: Jimmer Fredette on Mike Conley: He was a pest defensively and incredible in ball screens. He was a lefty who was actually better at floaters with his right hand, which made him a nightmare to guard.

clips.text: It's a few things. One of the things, obviously, is the rules of the Europe and Asia are very different. So, in Europe, I think it's four imports can be on the court at a time. An Asian import is basically anybody that's not from that country that you're in. clips.text: It is a team-oriented game, but where it differs is because it's only two imports on the court, a lot of times they're getting a lot of the motion ran for them and a lot of the actions are ran for them, opposed to you having equal attacks from four or five different other guys that can play. So, that's why you see the high-scoring outburst from these guys in China for a lot of times because it's not just running gun like people think it is.
